Dedication: ROBERT J. STOLLER, M.D., 1924-1991

Jos. Lichtenberg Editor-in-Chief

Jos. Lichtenberg

Jos. Lichtenberg  

Aaron Copland composed “Fanfare for the Common Man.” This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry is dedicated to an uncommon man. Robert Stoller took an often neglected route to psychoanalytic discovery. To learn about the variations in sexual practices, he eschewed looking to theory to illuminate his path, but turned directly to people instead. He invited people with a wide variety of sexual interests and orientations, many decidedly unusual, to tell him their experiences. Through his dedication to learn, understand, and empathize with them, he evoked their trust and they revealed to him personal information few other professionals have been privileged to hear. He respected their version of their lives, their motives, their need to self-deceive and obfuscate as well as reveal. Then he made his theory. Stoller's open mind to the novel and the puzzling and his direct involvement with people as the informational source for his inquiry allow us to place him solidly in the tradition of Freud.

Prologue

Estelle Shane PHD Editor and Morton Shane PHD Editor

Morton Shane

Morton Shane  

This issue is composed of articles in honor of and inspired by the 1989 volume Psychoanalysis and Motivation by Joseph Lichtenberg, a singularly important study for all of psychoanalysis and arguably Lichtenberg's most creative and comprehensive contribution to date. As Friedman writes in this issue, “Psychoanalysis and Motivation is a book for prolonged study not simply because it leaves scarcely any aspect of psychoanalysis untouched but because it does not settle for that breathtaking accomplishment.” Friedman goes on to state that rather than introducing in a general fashion his theory of motivational systems, Lichtenberg has contemplated “the details and difficulties … with a subtlety that is usually left to second- and third-generation students who have benefited from a long history of discussion and debate.” Although not all of the contributors to this issue share Friedman's most laudatory assessment, at the least each of them finds in this book a stimulus for thinking and rethinking psychoanalytic views on human motivation. And as issue editors, we can say that Lichtenberg's contribution is a tour de force of integration, both of the many theories of psychoanalysis extant in our pluralistic world and of correlated discoveries from related disciplines, most notably infant and toddler observation and experimentation and neurophysiological findings. In fact, the last chapter in Lichtenberg's volume, written by the neurophysiologist June Hadley, is a specific attempt to elucidate and correlate the neurophysiological underpinnings to the motivational systems proposed by Lichtenberg.

The first article in this issue, written by James L. Fosshage, articulates Lichtenberg's theory clearly. Fosshage presents his own assessment of Lichtenberg's overall schema, focusing on what he considers to be the most important clinical implications to be derived from it. Among the many thoughtful and pertinent observations Fosshage makes here, we mention only two in preview.

An Appreciative Response

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 18th Street NW Washington, DC 2009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

I am exceedingly gratified by the responses to Psychoanalysis and Motivation of the contributors to this issue. These responses indicate areas of shared agreement as well as serious questions I need to consider and challenges I need to meet. As Friedman states, my book is something closer to a textbook. Or, as one dear friend said to me with tongue in cheek, next time you write a book put some meat in it. The length and at times dense writing is the result of my belief that I needed to buttress my hypothesis with a mass of solid evidence since I am putting forward a psychoanalytic theory of motivation that departs in its complexity from any other. In addition, I needed to relate my ideas to earlier theoretical concepts that covered the same or similar territory. And I have used a systems theory that is richer and more dynamic that either “structures” or functions. We follow the progress of each of five motivational needs as a system self-organizes in response to innate and learned response patterns when the need is triggered, then self-stabilizes, then exists in dialectic tension within the system and with other systems for dominance of awareness, and finally undergoes progressive hierarchical rearrangement with maturation and increasing lived experience. I only sketched in the developmental pathways after infancy, and as I discuss, I lost some of the contributors in this part of my endeavor. But no contributors challenged the existence of any of the systems or proposed returning to a dual drive theory.

Dr. Lichtenberg is Director and Founding Member of the Institute of Contemporary Psychotherapy.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Estelle Shane PHD Editor and Morton Shane MD Editor

Morton Shane

Morton Shane  

We would like to end this volume of reflections on and appreciation for Joseph Lichtenberg's seminal—indeed, already classic—contribution, Psychoanalysis and Motivation, with an expression of our own personal gratitude to all of the contributors who have so generously responded to our invitation to join in this dialogue with the author. We would also, at this point, like to thank Joe Lichtenberg himself for his Appreciative Response and to restrict our brief closing comments to Lichtenberg's own closing article.

In his article, Lichtenberg not only answers all of the critical and admiring commentaries included in this volume with the same informative and respectful evenhandedness, but he also adds new observations that serve to extend our understanding of the application of his motivational systems. The most frequent concern expressed in these commentaries has been the equal status afforded each motivational system in relation to the others—not only in development, but throughout life, and particularly in the clinical situation. Lichtenberg, to our view, successfully addresses this concern. Gedo's point that the motivational systems as described by Lichtenberg only pertain directly to mode I in Gedo's own developmental schema, with higher form motivations such as morality left unaddressed, is responded to by acknowledging that further attention must be paid to the intricate interrelationship among the motivational systems as development proceeds. Lichtenberg further notes that in his succeeding volume, written in collaboration with Lachmann and Fosshage, as well as in his contribution to a collection by Wilson and Gedo, the motivational systems are further elaborated. Moreover, in Lichtenberg's discussion of our contribution to this volume, he adumbrates two developmental lines—generativity, in the attachment system, and ambition, in the exploratory-assertive system.

Channels of Communication and the Analytic Setup

John Gedo MD

John Gedo

680 N. Lake Shore Drive
Chicago, IL 60611

John Gedo  

There is much to be said in favor of performing tasks of daunting complexity, including the conduct of psychoanalyses, within a reliable framework—a set of conventions that may be taken for granted—in order to reduce to a relatively manageable number the variables that the practitioner has to monitor. Winnicott (1954), in referring to the conventions generally accepted by large sections of our community, called the almost banal results produced by these traditions—our liturgy, if you will—the “psychoanalytic situation.” Unlike the rituals of religion, however, no aspect of these conventions of ours is actually sacred. In America; we do not shake hands before and after each session, we do not provide analysands with warm coverlets; and, for that matter, we do not demand that they pay us in cash; yet these are routine aspects of the psychoanalytic situation in certain milieux abroad.

Perhaps no component of the psychoanalytic situation is as widely practiced as the use of the couch. Although this convention was originally dictated by the requirements of Freud's preanalytic “pressure technique,” wherein he strove to overcome the obstacles to the recollection of repressed mental contents by taking hold of the patient's head, it was retained when he changed the technique of treatment to that of relying first on directed and later on free associations.

Dr. Gedo has retired as Training and Supervising Analyst at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis. In various capacities, he has contributed fourteen volumes to the psychoanalytic literature.

Lichtenberg's Theory of Therapy

Joseph Weiss MD

Joseph Weiss

2420 Sutter Street San Francisco, CA 94115

Joseph Weiss  

Ienjoyed reading psychoanalysis and motivation. It is thoughtful, interesting, and carefully reasoned. The therapist who reads Lichtenberg's account of the maturation and expression of the five motivational systems in infancy and early childhood will acquire a heightened sense of his or her patient's varied motivations. By his careful delineation of these systems, Lichtenberg has broadened the developmental concepts on which self psychologists and other therapists may draw in their attempts to understand the motives of their patients.

In my discussion of Lichtenberg's (1989) Psychoanalysis and Motivation, I focus on his theory of therapy. I attempt to illuminate his theory by comparing it with a theory of therapy that I developed and that the Mount Zion Research Group (now known as the San Francisco Psychotherapy Research Group), which I co-direct with Harold Sampson, has investigated by formal research studies (Weiss, Sampson, and the Mt. Zion Psychotherapy Research Group, 1986).

Having worked for the last 25 years on developing my own understanding of the therapeutic process, I have no choice but to perceive Lichtenberg's theory through the lens of my own concepts. Also, I inevitably must discuss Lichtenberg's theory from the vantage point of an outsider. As I know from my own experience, a person on the outside can never understand a theory of therapy in the same way as someone who uses it in the daily work with his or her patients.

Lichtenberg's theory and mine have much in common.

Dr. Weiss is a Training Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute and Codirector, San Francisco Psychotherapy Research Group.

Prologue

F. Barth C.S.W. Issue Editor

F. Barth

F. Barth  

From the time psychoanalytic theory was first introduced, psychoanalysts have attempted to explain similarities and differences between women and men, masculinity and femininity. In some of his last comments on the subject, Freud (1933) wrote that what he had to say “about femininity … is certainly incomplete and fragmentary and does not always sound friendly…. If you want to know more about femininity, enquire from your own experiences of life, or turn to the poets, or wait until science can give you deeper and more coherent information” (p. 135).

Despite this disclaimer, most early psychoanalysts followed Freud in viewing both femininity and masculinity as derivative of psychosexual phenomena. Although there were those such as Karen Horney, Ernest Jones, and Melanie Klein, who disagreed with Freud's ideas about femininity from the beginning, few questioned his thinking about masculinity. Only in the past quarter of a century have psychoanalysts given serious consideration to ways of conceptualizing both femininity and masculinity other than those proffered by Freud and his followers.

Robert Stoller was a leader of this movement. Contemporary theories of masculine and feminine gender identity have been significantly influenced by his work. Utilizing data gathered from clinical and anthropological inquiries, he questioned Freud's conclusions and began to explore a variety of factors involved in the development of gender identity.

Stoller (1985) noted that gender identity (as differentiated from biologically determined sex) is a complex, multiply determined experience, which he described as “a dense mass of beliefs, an algebraic sum of ifs, buts, and ands—not an incontrovertible fact” (pp. 10-11).

The seven papers in this issue represent a sampling of contemporary psychoanalytic thinking about these beliefs.

F. Barth C.S.W. Issue Editor

F. Barth

F. Barth  

If one could find a single concept on which contemporary psychoanalysts with different theoretical persuasions might agree, it would probably be Pine's (1985) comment that “human developmental phenomena are endlessly complex” (p. 146). This is perhaps also one theme that runs through contemporary thinking about feminine and masculine gender identity and that can be found in the seven articles in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry.

The papers detail some of the complex constellations of dynamics involved in masculine and feminine gender identity. Although the various authors might disagree on some of the specifics, they all seem to agree that a variety of factors affect the gender identity of any single individual. Some of the authors have focused on the possibility that, while core gender identity may be established quite early, there is broader sense of what it means to be a man or a woman that changes over time, as an individual engages in the many developmental tasks that continue to affect her or his sense of self throughout the life cycle. To paraphrase (and extend) a concept of Steiner-Adair (1989), men and women in our culture struggle with numerous different images of feminine and masculine identity, and must find a way to satisfy “a quest for identity based on personhood rather than on gender-prescribed roles” (Steiner-Adair, 1989, pp. 155-156).

Contemporary research such as that described by Robinson and Biringen indicates that there are some specific innate behavioral differences between infant boys and girls, and that these differences may influence masculine and feminine gender identity. Yet they point out that it is not always easy to determine just how much of this behavior is constitutional and how much is influenced by the parents' (often unconscious) attitudes and expectations. Learning to Learn, Learning to Teach

Jonathan Schindelheim MD

Jonathan Schindelheim

750 Washington Street
Boston, MA 0211

Jonathan Schindelheim  

The aspect of psychoanalytic supervision that I would like to address is that of learning—or, to be more accurate, not learning. I think of it as the gulf between knowing something in the head, or even by heart, and having it in one's bones, available for use. As I tried to learn from my supervisors throughout my training, I experienced this dichotomy week after week, month after month, for years. The lesson of one particular supervision highlighted it for me. When I was finally able to integrate that lesson into the very fabric of the supervision, my understanding evolved to the point that I began to solve my riddle. My subsequent discussions with residents and medical students suggested that the lesson's message had broadened my perspective on both sides of the supervisory equation.

When I began to work with patients in analytic training, I recognized feelings from my first experiences as a psychotherapist. Difficulties from those early days reappeared as well.

Jonathan Schindelheim, M.D. is Assistant Professor and Director of Medical Education, Department of Psychiatry, Tufts University School of Medicine, New England Medical Center; faculty, Psychoanalytic Institute of New England, East.

Supervision and Its Discontents: A Discussion of the Foregoing Papers

Jerome Katz MD

Jerome Katz

Box 829
Topeka, KS 66601

Jerome Katz  

If psychoanalysis is among the impossible professions, supervision may well be its most impossible aspect. Supervisors are charged with promoting the professional and personal growth of the supervisee, as well as with responsibility for the welfare of the patient. They find themselves positioned in a number of complex triadic relationships: patient-supervisee-training analyst, patient-supervisee-supervisor. They may be the target of transferences displaced from the supervisee's training analyst. At times they may be the recipient of what could be called institutional transferences, including the needs/wishes of the candidate to follow the rules of the institute and aspects of competition, power struggles, and dissensions among supervisors and training analysts. Or, they may be pushed by the wish to take over and thus interfere with the supervisee's making his own discoveries and ideas about interventions. Optimally, they should avoid leaping in with their own “Aha!” or admirable interpretation, but instead allow the student to find his own way. Similarly, they must resist the temptation to be authoritarian or to simply pour information into unknowing ears or insist that theirs is the only way, the right way to do things. While they model for the supervisee how an analyst listens and thinks, they need to help the supervisee to develop his own style and not simply to ape or identify with theirs. Supervisors may need to deal delicately with the supervisee's insistence on doing things the way his own analyst did.

Jerome B. Katz, M.D. (retired) was a Training and Supervising Analyst, and Director and Chairman of the Education Committee of the Topeka Institute for Psychoanalysis.

Love's Labour's Lost

I

There is told the story of a princely scholar who binds himself and his chosen associates to a quasi-monastic scheme of life only to discover that their “little academe, still and contemplative in living art,” is quickly overcome by their “own affections and the huge army of the world's desires.” No, I am not talking about one of our august colleague's struggle against transference and countertransference, but about the very first play written by the great bard. Young adulthood spans a generation. Within those years boys become men as they struggle with the powerful issues of autonomy, intimacy, and parenthood. In an attempt to illustrate this process, placing special emphasis on the relationship between fathers and sons. I will present clinical material from the treatment of two men, one at the beginning of young adulthood, the other at the end. Then I will use this clinical material to organize my theoretical comments around several developmental tasks that, in my opinion, best describe male experience during these years.

Jim

I first met Jim when he was 9 years old. At that time his parents brought him for evaluation because of a general sense of unhappiness, temper tantrums, and difficulty in making friends. Evaluation revealed a bright, well-organized, neurotic youngster, and a recommendation for analysis was made and accepted. During our 3 years together we were able to work in-depth on all aspects of Jim's neurosis. At its core were typical infantile sexual issues and a particularly intense positive oedipal conflict, that is, aggressive feelings and fantasies about father, whom Jim experienced as distant, demanding and ungiving.

Calvin Colarusso, M.D. is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry and Director of the Child Psychiatry Residency Training Program at the University of California at San Diego. He is a Training and Supervising Analyst in Adult and Child Psychoanalysis at the San Diego Psychoanalytic Institute.

Patsy Turrini M.S.S. and Dale Mendell PHD

Dale Mendell

1995 Oakwood Avenue
Merrick, NY 11560

102 Overlook Terrace
East Hills, NY 11577

Dale Mendell  

Summary and Conclusions

Maternal developmental lines originate from good-enough endowment, innate wishes, and experience with good mothering. Early preoedipal structures related to symbiotic fantasies of oneness, the need for completion of self, and omnipotent perfective magic wishes either contribute to the development of, or are organizers of, standards and goals that become part of the adult maternal ego ideal and patterns of adult caretaking. Other variables that contribute to material development but are not described in this paper include specific identifications, idiosyncratic fantasies, reparative and masochistic resolutions, normal defenses, and the effects of traumatic childhood events. Early maternal structures become an aspect of the small girl's emerging sense of gender identity, and influence typical developing defenses against aggression.

Psychoanalytic theorists frequently regard normative preoedipal derivatives such as those described in this paper as pathological. We make a distinction between normal derivatives and pathogenic variants such as symbiotic fixation and altruistic surrender (Edward, Ruskin, and Turrini, 1991, p. 268). If, during psychotherapy, normative

108

affective and content states in mothers are treated as pathological, depression or withdrawal may ensue, and maternal aspects of the gendered self will remain unexplored.

We suggest that while the illusions that are part and parcel of preoedipal structuralization provide necessary motivation for child rearing, they are also sources of normative pain when the adult woman is confronted with an actual rather than a fantasized child. Therefore, we expect sadness and depression in women in reaction to frustration and disappointment in achieving idealized maternal expectations.

John Gedo MD

John Gedo

680 N. Lake Shore Drive Chicago, IL 60611

John Gedo  

Although there is general consensus that psychoanalysis is a science of motivations, there is much less agreement about how motivation should actually be defined. According to the dictionary, the word refers to whatever impels a person to act, or more narrowly, to act volitionally. In Freud's metapsychology, the focus shifted to mental acts, and motivation became the force that sets the mental apparatus in motion—what psychoanalysis viewed from the “dynamic” viewpoint. This conceptualization presented depth psychology in the language of physics, particularly that of the late 19th-century science of electricity. In parallel with measurements in terms of volts, ohms, and amperes, Freud relied on concepts of forces, resistances, and energies. In other words, a dynamics of motives implicitly required complementary concepts of structure and intensities. Freud outlined such a theoretical schema between 1892 and 1900, from “Sketches for the Preliminary Communication of 1893” to chapter 7 of The Interpretation of Dreams.

For two decades thereafter, Freud tried to define the nature of psychological forces in terms of innate, constitutionally determined potentialities he called instinctual drives (in German, Trieb). At first these were subdivided into self-preservative and sexual motives; because this classification failed to account for narcissistic issues (Freud, 1914), the libidinal drives were further differentiated into narcissistic and object libido. New York, NY 10025

Sabrina Wolfe  

Gender Identity Disorder (GID) of childhood is a very rare syndrome, first classified in DSM-III, characterized by a persistent and determined wish to be the opposite gender coupled with an intense dislike of one's own gender. Boys with the syndrome are referred for clinical evaluation far more frequently than girls by a ratio of approximately 5 to 1 (Zucker and Green, 1992). The onset of the disorder almost invariably occurs during the ages of 2 to 4, and once established, it is surprisingly stable and usually proves refractory to all but the most intensive psychodynamic and family interventions. Extensive biomedical research has failed to document any chromosomal or hormonal abnormalities associated with the disorder.

Typical is the case of Colin, a 3-year-old boy reported in detail elsewhere (Coates, Friedman, and Wolfe, 1991). Colin had frequently dressed in his mother's clothes since the age of 2. He was intensely interested in jewelry and makeup and would spend long periods of time cross-dressed in front of a mirror.

Susan Coates, Ph.D. is Director of the Childhood Gender Identity Center in the Department of Psychiatry of St. Luke's/Roosevelt Hospital in New York City; Sabrina Wolfe, Ph.D. is Associate Director.

We would like to express our appreciation to John Kerr, whose many probing questions led us to refine our thinking and sharpen our formulations, and to Larry Friedman and William Byne for their suggestions on an earlier draft of this paper.

Scott Goldsmith MD

Scott Goldsmith

1300 York Avenue
Box 16

Scott Goldsmith  

Summary

Within the framework of the oedipal complex formulated here, a homosexual boy is at a disadvantage in attempting to identify with other men, and is forced into a relationship with his mother that makes separation from her difficult and that may distort his view of femininity. A consideration of the vicissitudes of these difficulties offers a number of insights into the development of the homosexual child. In particular, it sheds light on some problems he may have in consolidating his gender identity, and in attempting to coordinate his masculinity and femininity to pursue a love relationship.

As I hope I have demonstrated, the clarification of these difficulties should be considered an important task for psychotherapists in their work with homosexual men. Clarification of the oedipal dynamics outlined here may coincide with a patient's ability to enjoy more freely intimate relationships with other men, and to renegotiate relationships with significant others, particularly with parents. Simultaneously, it may lead to an ability to traditionally “feminine” impulses less ambivalently, and to experience masculinity more authentically. Further clinical research in this area will be of considerable interest.

The Couch as a Protective Shield for the Analyst

George Moraitis MD

George Moraitis

180 North Michigan Avenue
Chicago, IL 60601

George Moraitis  

In recent years, Freud's theoretical and clinical propositions have been challenged or reformulated by a number of psychoanalytic scholars and clinicians. The changes represent a shift in the focus of psychoanalytic investigation, both clinically and conceptually, from the oedipal to the more archaic, from the verbal to the nonverbal, from the intrapsychic to the interpersonal and to the intersubjective, and from the study of the patient apart from the analyst to the study of the patient-analyst dyad in which both participants receive more or less equal attention. This change in focus has provided a very different perspective of the journey into the unconscious from the one that Freud had originally conceptualized.

The traditional analytic setup, in which the patient lies on the couch with the analyst sitting behind it, was designed by Freud as an intrinsic part of the journey into the dynamic unconscious and the recovery of the repressed. Given the much wider scope of many contemporary psychoanalytic theories, it is rather surprising that practically nothing new has been proposed to replace or modify the traditional psychoanalytic setup in general and the use of the couch in particular.

Regardless of the school(s) of thought within the boundaries of which the analyst conducts the analysis, the use of the couch remains the common denominator about which there seems to be very little open controversy among psychoanalysts. Thus, the use of the couch seems to be one of the most enduring of Freud's recommendations.

Dr. Moraitis is Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, and Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, Northwestern University.

A Reassessment of the Couch in Psychoanalysis

James Grotstein MD

James Grotstein

522 Dalehurst Avenue
Los Angeles, CA 90024

James Grotstein  

The use of the couch for the treatment of mental disorders has a history that long antedates Freud's initial employment of it. The ancient Greeks apparently practiced an equivalent form of psychoanalysis that was characterized by the use of the couch; dream analysis; and the employment of rhetoric, dialectic, and catharsis (Entralgo, 1970; Simon, 1978). It is not clear what their rationale was for the use of the couch. As we now know, Freud's suggestion that the patient use the couch was largely for personal reasons. He did not want to be observed while thinking about the patient's free associations, and he also believed that the patient, by feeling more comfortable lying down, would be able to tap into deeper layers of preconscious phantasies.

Freud apparently never realized that he had, in effect, discovered the right brain hemisphere! When a person lies down and does not make eye contact with the other person in the discourse, he or she seems to activate a cerebral hemispheric shift in terms of modes of data processing from the left to the right in right-handed persons and vice versa for left-handed persons. Interestingly, researchers in infant observation also noted that there was a noticeable difference in infant alertness when the infant was observed sitting up as contrasted with lying down. This shift in the alertness of consciousness corresponded to electroencephalographic changes in states of alertness and also to a hemispheric shift.

Dr. Grotstein is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the University of California at Los Angeles, and Training and Supervising Analyst at the Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Institute.

Sameness and Difference: Toward an “Overinclusive” Model of Gender Development

Jessica Benjamin PHD

Jessica Benjamin

228 West 22nd Street
New York, NY 10011

Jessica Benjamin  

The idea of gender development has of necessity been linked to the notion of coming to terms with difference. What has changed in contemporary thinking is the meaning of sexual difference, which is no longer equated with anatomical difference. Assimilating the meaning of sexual difference(s) and assuming a position in relation to it are no longer seen as triggered by the discovery of anatomical facts. To some degree, however, psychoanalytic assumptions about the character of gender difference have not wholly been liberated from the naturalizing tendency in Freud's thought, although in a more covert and subtle form. This form consists of a tendency to view the realization of difference as if it were more significant than, or detached from, the realization of likeness. The implicit assumption in differentiation theory is that acknowledging difference has a higher value, is a later achievement, and is more difficult than recognizing likeness. The neglected point is that the difficulty lies in assimilating difference without repudiating likeness, that is, in straddling the space between the opposites. It is easy enough to give up one side of a polarity in order to oscillate toward the other side. What is difficult is to attain a notion of difference—being unlike—without giving up a sense of commonality, of being “like.

Jessica Benjamin, Ph.D. is on the faculty of the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy and of the Graduate Faculty Program in Psychoanalytic Studies at the New School for Social Research. Her volume of essays Like Subjects and Love Objects will appear in 1995.

Lawrence Friedman  

Joseph lichtenberg's (1989) psychoanalysis and motivation is a book for prolonged study not simply because it leaves scarcely any aspect of psychoanalysis untouched but because it does not settle for that breathtaking accomplishment. Where one would have expected the author to introduce his theory in a general fashion, he has instead written something closer to a textbook, contemplating the details and difficulties and working out the issues with a subtlety that is usually left to second- and third-generation students who have benefited from a long history of discussion and debate. On re-reading, one keeps discovering that questions in afterthought have been already dealt with. I am far from certain that the issues I call attention to are not better discussed in the book itself.

Of the many facets of development, mind, and therapy that are handled in Lichtenberg's theory, I will concentrate on his solution to what might be called the Problem of the Main Meaning. I refer to the problem of how to determine—and what it means to determine—a particular preeminent significance in a patient's behavior or speech. That is one half of the continuous task of an analyst or psychotherapist—the other half being how to profitably respond to what looks like the main meaning in light of other of the patient's meanings.

Although new psychoanalytic theories almost always advance new main meanings, Lichtenberg's stands alone, I think, in finding detailed justification in both basic science and the dramatic highlights of practice.

Dr. Friedman is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry and a member of the History of Psychiatry section of the Department of Psychiatry, Cornell University Medical College.

The Application of Lichtenberg's Five Motivational Systems to the Analysis of Mother-Infant Interaction

B. Campbell PHD , Donald Silver MD , Kerry Novick , Jack Novick PHD , Mary Mittlestaedt RNC and Anne Walton BA

Anne Walton

29994 Northwestern Highway
 Farmington Hills, MI 48334

Anne Walton  

Summary

We have reported a preliminary research effort to apply Lichtenberg's five motivational systems to the analysis of videotaped mother-infant interactional data. The work required viewing each segment at least

490

10 times, focusing each time on one member of the dyad and assessing one motivational system. The richness of this method is also its fault: The method generates considerable data. It is not a simple system; the definitions and behavioral categories are not discrete. Future work would be served by creating a coding system that could be utilized by pairs of judges comparing and contrasting their impressions in an effort to reach agreement. The repetitive process of examining single episodes of mother-infant interaction enhances clinical understanding of the expression and effect of motivational needs on the overall development of the individual and can be extended to the work with adult analytic patients.

In summary, we were able to apply Lichtenberg's motivational systems concepts, derived from clinical and theoretical psychoanalysis, to observational research data. The conflicts of mother-infant interaction, within each partner and between the two, were sharply elucidated when we looked at behavior from the point of view of each motivational system. This enriched our understanding of the unfolding mutual influences between the adolescent mothers and their babies, which could also be applied to healthy pairs, and allowed for enhanced description of fluctuations and patterning among the motivational systems.

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 18th Street, NW

Joseph Lichtenberg  

On the Couch

Along with other adolescents of the 1940s, I was drawn by the lore of the Freudian revolution to become a pioneer explorer of the new frontier of the psyche. I intended to be a scientist, a doctor, and a psychoanalyst. The couch was to be my laboratory table for dissection and study, my operating table for surgical cure, and my magical bed for day and night dreams. When I began my personal analysis while a medical student, I approached the couch with awe; I envisioned it as a shrine for the realization of my ambitions. I can easily recreate my uncertainty as I first ventured onto that horizontal slab on which I found, not a person, but a ceiling to stare at as I tried my skill at “free association.” I can remember my thrill as I got the hang of it and began to touch the depths of feelings I was pleased to discover I was capable of experiencing despite my intellectual veneer. Getting onto the couch became routine and welcome; getting off was another story. Especially at those times when I felt like I was deeply into something, I was reluctant to leave and even more reluctant to have to reachieve verticality and equilibrium as I dried my tears and reassembled my face-for-the-world.

Dr. Lichtenberg is Director and Founding Member of the Institute of Contemporary Psychotherapy.

Looking, Listening, and the Couch

Leo Sadow MD

Leo Sadow

151 N. Michigan Avenue, Suite 904
Chicago, IL 60601

Leo Sadow  

Some months after the beginning of her analysis, a patient suddenly turned her head to look at me and, with surprise and disappointment, said that she thought I might be sexually excited. During the course of the analysis, we referred back to this bit of “acting in” in various ways. But of the most interest to my current purpose is an observation she made shortly before the end of the analysis about her “take” on my earlier relaxed and alert attitude. She said, “You seemed to be listening with everything you had.” Indeed, I had been listening with everything I had. The analysis was long and complicated, and the transference was sometimes highly eroticized, sometimes untrusting, sometimes rageful, sometimes hateful, sometimes loving. But what ultimately drove it was the conviction that I listened so intently that I could join with her in understanding her many-faceted life.

Every psychoanalyst would agree that such listening is an essential part of the analytic process, but I suspect that there would be less agreement about just what constitutes such a psychological state and how it is best facilitated. Specifically, what part does the patient's recumbent position on the couch play? Can we achieve the same thing sitting vis-à-vis? Has the couch become an anachronism—or more, an icon, a relic of our history—to which we make our obligatory obeisance? Or does it really play a vital role in analytic work? Could I have listened with everything I had if my patient and I had been comfortably seated facing one another?

Dr. Sadow is Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Illinois College of Medicine.

I am indebted to Dr. George Moraitis for his help in writing this paper.

The Couch: Reflections From an Interactional View of Analysis

Roy Aruffo MD

Roy Aruffo

5300 San Jacinto, Suite 105
Houston, TX 77004

Roy Aruffo  

Part of the human condition is the need for structure. The couch, integral to psychoanalytic technique, is part of the structure of psychoanalytic treatment. Its use sometimes provides the psychoanalyst with the sense of knowing what should be done, how it should be done, and how best to observe the unfolding transference.

The psychoanalyst's respect for the structure of the psychoanalytic situation distinguishes psychoanalysis from countless other therapies. Yet, at times, the analyst's respect for this structure overrides other considerations dictated by logic and common sense. When this occurs, psychoanalysis is defined not by its essence but by technical considerations such as the number of sessions per week, duration of treatment, and whether the couch is used. I strongly believe that ultimately what is analytic can only be defined by the particular analytic process related to it.

Some would argue that whether a treatment is considered “analytic” is immaterial, and certainly that is true for the patient. But for organized psychoanalysis, for being certified, promoted, and graduated, those issues can be crucial. An example occurred when an analytic candidate's graduation paper was refused because the patient was seen only three times a week; this factor and because the patient sat up were said to disqualify the treatment as analytic, yet the patient and analyst were engaged in a clear analytic process.

Dr. Aruffo is Training and Supervising Analyst, Houston/Galveston Psychoanalytic Institute, and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Arkansas, Baylor College of Medicine, and University of Texas at Houston.

The Analytic Couch: Facilitator or Sine Qua Non?

Jacob Jacobson MD

Jacob Jacobson

1636 16th Street
Boulder, Colorado 80302

Jacob Jacobson  

Sine qua non means literally “without which not” and is usually translated as “indispensable” (Mawson, 1975). In the course of the history of psychoanalysis, the use of the couch has moved on a continuum from incidental adjunct, to helpful facilitator, to “without which not.” Each such shift has marked a change in our understanding of psychoanalytic technique and of the place of the couch within it.

As Freud pointed out in 1913, the use of the couch was almost accidental at the outset—an accident of history in the hypnosis heritage of psychoanalysis and an accident of history in Freud's personal distaste for being looked at for long hours each day. As Freud (1913) put it in “On Beginning the Treatment”:

Before I wind up these remarks on beginning analytic treatment, I must say a word about a certain ceremonial which concerns the position in which the treatment is carried out. I hold to the plan of getting the patient to lie on a sofa while I sit behind him out of his sight. This arrangement has a historical basis; it is the remnant of the hypnotic method out of which psycho-analysis was evolved. But it deserves to be maintained for many reasons. The first is a personal motive, but one which others may share with me. I cannot put up with being stared at by other people for eight hours a day (or more) [pp. 133-134].

Dr. Jacobson is Training and Supervising Analyst, Denver Institute for Psychoanalysis, and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Colorado Health Sciences Center.

The Analytic Couch as Transference Object

Richard Waugaman MD

Richard Waugaman

Chestnut Lodge
500 W. Montgomery Avenue
Rockville, MD 20850

Richard Waugaman  

A woman walked into my office for an initial consultation, took one look at my analytic couch, and exclaimed, “That's not a couch—it's a bed!” Albeit dramatically, she was exemplifying a universal process: All patients imbue the couch with transference meaning. For our patients, as in the popular mind, the analytic couch is the quintessential symbol of psychoanalysis, with all its connotations, whether common or idiosyncratic. Another woman once wondered if I ever napped on the couch. For me to do so, she added, would seem “sacrilegious.” The couch clearly had an almost sacred significance for her. She was capturing the widespread idealization of the couch that is displaced from an idealizing transference toward the analyst and the analytic process.

First, it may be helpful to clarify my use of the word transference. We usually apply this term to feelings and reactions toward a person, especially the analyst. However, we sometimes extend the term transference to include things, not just people—for example, when we refer to institutional transferences. Searles (1960) has written extensively about the transference meaning of various aspects of the nonhuman environment. The analytic couch is a central feature of the nonhuman environment within the analyst's office. In this article, I explore some of the many transference meanings the couch may assume.

Dr. Waugaman is Training and Supervising Analyst, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute; and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Georgetown University School of Medicine.

Brief Notes on Using the Couch

Ernest Wolf MD

Ernest Wolf

1333 Tower Road
Winnetka, IL 60093

Ernest Wolf  

The couch has become the analyst's trademark and logo. The conflation of analyst and couch into the sanctioned semblance of psychoanalytic treatment appears to have been accepted by psychoanalysts as much as by the public. It is exceedingly rare to see the routine use of the couch either challenged or affirmed in the psychoanalytic professional literature. The use of the couch seems to be taken for granted when psychoanalysis is the treatment of choice. To be sure, not every analyst does in fact position every patient on the couch regardless of other considerations. There are some psychoanalysts who occasionally, but rarely, will analyze their patients in a sit-up, face-to-face position when this seems indicated. Except for omitting the use of the couch, such analyses may be technically indistinguishable from the traditional analytic methods.

The origin of the recumbent position in psychoanalysis is derived from hypnosis, its ancestor in medical practice. The procedure of having the patient lie on a sofa while the analyst sat behind the patient out of sight was thought by Freud (1913) to be a ceremonial and historical remnant of the hypnotic method. He thought it deserved to be maintained for a number of reasons, some of which he listed. They bear repeating.

First, Freud said he could not put up with being stared at by other people for eight hours a day or more. Second, he did not wish the expressions on his face to give the patient material either for interpretation or to influence him or her.

Dr. Wolf is Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, and Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, Northwestern University.

Epilogue

Joshua Levy Issue Editor and Alan Kindler M.B.B.S. Issue Editor

Alan Kindler

Alan Kindler  

Several common themes are expressed in various ways in these papers. The themes we wish to highlight and elaborate on in this discussion include the nature of the learning alliance in supervision, the continuing struggle to strike a balance between teaching and treating, the pleasures of supervision, and the need for training of supervisors.

The Learning Alliance

Implicitly or explicitly, all of our contributors touched on the significance of the learning alliance in supervision. Many authors, including Dewald (1987) and Wallerstein (1981), have proposed and developed this concept as a dimension of the supervisory relationship analogous to the “therapeutic alliance” in the psychoanalytic relationship. In both domains, these alliances depend on the availability, reliability, honesty, responsiveness, and caring of the helping partner. And in both situations the alliance is expressed and experienced at the conscious and unconscious levels. To those qualities in the supervisor that contribute to the learning alliance in the supervisory relationship we would append sensitivity to the candidate's self-esteem regulation, particularly to his or her propensity to shame experiences related to the inevitable exposure of mistakes and shortcomings.

We concur that these are essential components of the supervisory learning alliance, but wish to propose that these factors be placed in a broader context that includes the supervisor's constant attention to the candidate's level of development as an analyst, strengths and vulnerabilities, and sense of self. All of these factors will influence the candidate's performance in clinical practice and in supervision at any moment. We have in mind here a problem-focused approach based on a global appreciation of the candidate as a learning person.

Supervision for Fun and Profit: Or How to Tell If the Fun is Profitable

Herbert Schlesinger PHD

Herbert Schlesinger

65 Fifth Avenue
New York, NY 10003

Herbert Schlesinger  

Amore narrowly descriptive and, certainly, more dignified title might be, “Diagnosis and Evaluation in Psychoanalytic Supervision.” But I wanted to allude to the spirit of my intentions, which is that the intrinsic pleasures in supervising, in participating in the growth and development of a younger colleague, are matched by a new set of responsibilities. I chose the more fanciful title because neither evaluation nor, to a lesser extent, diagnosis are generally thought of as intrinsic to the functions of an analyst. Indeed, they are commonly thought of as alien to the spirit of psychoanalysis. After all, the analyst is expected to listen nonjudgmentally, and although the matters that interest the analyst are distributed among diagnostic categories, they are not captured by formal diagnosis. And yet, the analyst when supervising must find a place for both functions in his or her repertoire. Is there a way in which these functions essential to supervising can be found congenial to the analyst within the supervisor? A digression is necessary before addressing this question directly.

Background

Our working assumption as psychoanalytic teachers and supervisors is that both the science and the art of doing psychoanalysis can be taught. And while that is true, it is more to the point to say that they can be learned.

Alfred J. and Monette C. Professor of Psychology, Emeritus, Graduate Faculty of Political and Social Sciences, New School for Social Research; Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

George Moraitis Issue Editor

George Moraitis

George Moraitis  

This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry addresses a topic that is perhaps the least controversial in psychoanalysis. Since 1912, when Freud made his famous recommendations about the use of the couch in psychoanalytic treatment, psychoanalysts have by and large been committed to the classical psychoanalytic setup, regardless of the school of psychoanalytic thought they adhere to.

Freud did not have to elaborate at length in order to persuade the analyst to use the couch. As a matter of fact, he hardly wrote anything on the subject after his original recommendations in 1912. Other psychoanalytic authors have, from time to time, discussed the issue of the patient's resistance to lying on the couch and elaborated on the meanings patients attached to that experience. Generally speaking, there seems to be an implicit consensus among psychoanalysts that using the couch in psychoanalytic treatment constitutes the sine qua non of the whole enterprise. In the absence of any open controversy, the reader may wonder about the purpose of this publication.

Actually, it is precisely this “silent consensus” that attracted my attention to this subject. It seemed to me somewhat paradoxical that, given all the changes introduced in psychoanalytic clinical theory during the last 25 years, no new rationales have been offered for using the couch in psychoanalysis and no questions have been raised about the relevance of Freud's original propositions.

As long as the psychoanalyst maintains strict adherence to Freud's original definition of the basic aim of psychoanalytic treatment—bringing the dynamic unconscious closer to consciousness—the usefulness of the couch remains clinically and conceptually indisputable.

This, however, may not be the case when the psychoanalytic process is conceptualized in the light of more contemporary psychoanalytic theories.

Alvin Frank MD

Alvin Frank

7751 Carondelet, Suite 801

Alvin Frank  

Nature is nowhere accustomed more openly to display her secret mysteries than in cases where she shows traces of her workings apart from the beaten path…. For it has been found, in almost all things, that what they contain of useful or applicable nature is hardly perceived unless we are deprived of them, or they become deranged in some way.

William Harvey, 1651

How droll that one of psychoanalysis's two clinical fundamentals should receive more attention as an icon than a technical dimension. In fact, even in most indexed references, the term couch is used to mean psychoanalysis itself. Is it that collaboration with the recommendation to lie down while revealing one's inner thoughts and feelings is a universally eventless, rarely complicated procedure? That would be surprising, considering the frequency with which we hear informally of patients' struggles with using the couch. And even Freud's (1913) first recommendation of this procedure cited resistance. Yet the couch seems more or less taken for granted and receives only cursory mention in textbooks and rare clinical articles.

What goes into the importance of the couch to the analyst? It is axiomatic that not looking at each other frees each analytic partner. In both participants, processes of inner realization are facilitated, in one by not viewing and in the other by not being viewed.

Dr. Frank is Training and Supervising Analyst, St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute, and Professor of Clinical Psychiatry, St. Louis University.

An Expansion of Motivational Theory:

Lichtenberg's Motivational Systems Model

James Fosshage PHD

James Fosshage

330 West 58th Street New York, NY 10019

James Fosshage  

A theory of motivation is at the core of each psychoanalytic model. It fundamentally shapes our developmental view of a person from infancy to senescence. It addresses the “why” questions concerning human behavior and experience. It serves in the clinical arena as the central organizing fulcrum and underpinning of our understandings and explanations. The importance of motivational theory clearly cannot be overstated.

Integrating infant studies, a vast range of empirical research, and clinical evidence, Lichtenberg has taken up the monumental task of developing a comprehensive motivational theory. The unifying goal that he set for himself was “to define motivational systems that exist in early infancy, persist in altered forms throughout life, and characterize observable changes in motivational dominance in an analytic session” (Lichtenberg, 1988, p. 60). In proposing five motivational systems in his book Psychoanalysis and Motivation, Lichtenberg (1989), in my opinion, provided us with the most complex and comprehensive motivational theory extant in psychoanalysis today.

Motivation refers generally to “the process of initiating, sustaining and directing psychological or physical activities” (Goldenson, 1984, p. 472). Phenomenologically motivations are experienced in a shifting kaleidoscope of desires, urges, aims, and strivings.

Dr. Fosshage is a Board Director and Faculty Member, National Institute for the Psychotherapies (NYC); Core Faculty Member, Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity (NYC); Faculty Member and Supervising Analyst, New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis.

“May I Bring My Newborn Baby to My Analytic Hour?”: One Analyst's Experience With This Request

Maxine Anderson MD

Maxine Anderson

2107 Elliott Avenue
Suite 310
Seattle, WA 98121

Maxine Anderson  

Most analysts who have been in practice for more than a few years have encountered situations that challenge the “rules” that we felt we learned during analytic training about the use of the couch and other elements of the analytic frame. Having experience in both the ego-psychology point of view and the British object-related point of view, and thinking of myself as quite clear and firm in my expectations of patients using the couch, I have encountered in three rather similar cases a puzzling situation that colleagues may find of interest: twice during my eight years of study and practice in London, and again upon returning to practice locally following my London stay, an analytic patient has asked insistently to bring her newborn baby to her analytic sessions for what was in each instance a period of several months. On each occasion, both at the time and in retrospect, I felt that allowing this parameter was quite appropriate and here, focusing in detail upon the third case encountered, I will detail why. As I am sure that colleagues have faced some of the same pressures from patients, I hope my notation about this clinical situation will be of interest.

A woman (whom I call P) in her mid-thirties, an interior decorator deserted by her husband, came to analysis for a number of reasons, but it soon became evident that her core issue revolved around the central feeling that no one understood or wished to understand her feelings and her point of view.

Dr. Anderson is Training and Supervising Analyst at the Seattle Institute of Psychoanalysis and Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, University of Washington.

Multiple Interactive Processes in Psychoanalytic Supervision

Eva Lester MD and Brian Robertson MD

Brian Robertson

1025 Pine Avenue W.
Montreal, Quebec H3A 1A1

Brian Robertson  

It is generally agreed that the personal analysis of the candidate and the supervised analyses during training constitute the essence of psychoanalytic education. Both are “enabling” processes, different from the simpler transmission of knowledge in the form of psychoanalytic seminars, the long established tradition in psychoanalytic institutes.

Psychoanalytic supervision repeatedly has been the subject of discussion among analytic teachers, and there exists a substantial literature on it. A short historical outline herein will trace the major themes in the evolution of thinking on the subject. The thesis of this paper is that supervision is an interactive process with multiple reverberations among candidate, patient, and supervisor, as well as among candidate, training (personal) analyst, and supervisor. We believe that the dichotomy between “teach” and “treat,” as articulated in the literature, is artificial and that strict adherence to such dichotomous thinking does not promote the enabling aspects of psychoanalytic supervision. In most cases the candidates are not aware of their countertransference to the patient, or are reluctant to discuss any personal reaction, concentrating instead on reporting the material as “objectively” as possible.

Eva P. Lester, M.D. is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Canadian Institute of Psychoanalysis. She is a Professor of Psychiatry at McGill University Medical School.

Brian M. Robertson, M.D. is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Canadian Institute of Psychoanalysis, and an Associate Professor of Psychiatry at McGill University Medical School.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

George Moraitis Issue Editor

George Moraitis

George Moraitis  

Several general conclusions can be extracted from the preceding papers.

The couch is used consistently by all contributors, regardless of theoretical orientation.

All contributors appreciate the need (a) to analyze the patient's reluctance to use the couch whenever it appears and (b) not to coerce the patient into using it.

While all contributors reported that some of their patients sat up during certain periods of their analyses, only one (Jacobson) reported that he analyzed a patient sitting up all the way through and still considered it a bona fide analysis.

New rationales are evolving, both in the direction of using the couch (Grotstein, Sadow, Wolf) and in the direction of not using it (Gedo, Lichtenberg), while Freud's rationale continues to be the basic reference for suitable cases.

None of the contributors claimed empirical knowledge of conducting an analysis without the use of the couch for experimental purposes. All empirical knowledge without the use of the couch is derived from patients who refused to go along with the analyst's recommendations. This constitutes a select group of patients about which no general conclusions can be drawn.

Obviously, a good deal remains inconclusive or even contradictory. Given the nature of the subject under consideration, this is unavoidable. Nonetheless, I hope that some important questions have been raised that will direct more attention to this important and sensitive subject.

In this paper we consider gender role/identity disorder, its nature, its etiology, and the degree to which it is changeable, with or without the aid of psychotherapy.

We begin with a clinical illustration concerning a boy suffering from a gender disorder. The child has been observed only indirectly through the treatment of his mother, Dr. W, in therapy with one of us (E.S.) for several years. Therefore, our focus will not be on E.S.'s patient, Dr. W, but on her son, Patrick, who has been a chronic concern for his mother since her treatment began. Patrick was 3 years old when his mother, Dr. W, started therapy. He had an older sister, Carolyn, whom the mother was quite attached to and identified with. Dr. W had wanted desperately to have another girl and so was quite disappointed when Patrick was born, but was soon after, even during Patrick's early infancy, considerably mollified when she noted how much like Carolyn Patrick seemed to be. She saw Patrick as having a “feminine sensibility”—unlike her husband, whom Dr.

In Memoriam: Merton Gill, M.D., 1914-1994

Jos. Lichtenberg Editor-in-Chef

Jos. Lichtenberg

Jos. Lichtenberg  

With the death of Merton Gill, Psychoanalytic Inquiry has lost a wonderful contributor and supporter. In 1984, Merton worked with Mel Bornstein to turn out a stellar Commentary on his and Irwin Hoffman's Analysis of Transference. Speaking at the American Psychoanalytic Association Meet-the-Author, Merton acknowledged that through responding to the essays in the journal issue, he reconsidered some of his points of view. The brilliance of Merton lay not in his conceptualizations, great as they were in ego psychology and later in social constructivism, but in his reconceptualizations. Merton could carry an idea to its logical limits and recognize when he had exploded the boundaries of its worth. That is a rare form of brilliance—a true follower of Freud.

At a meeting of the International Psychoanalytic Association held in New York many years ago, I was asked to chair a discussion group on reconstruction. I ran into Merton at a cocktail party the night before and he told me he was coming to my workshop. In my instant awe I said, “Oh, no, Merton! You should be running it.” “No,” he said, “Joe, you run—I heckle.” Our field will dearly miss so remarkably constructive a heckler.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Joshua Levy Issue Editor and Alan Kindler M.B.B.S. Issue Editor

Alan Kindler

Alan Kindler  

The role of the teacher is often a conservative one. In addition to the transmission of knowledge and techniques, teachers are frequently entrusted with the preservation of the values and traditions of their discipline. Nowhere has this been truer than in psychoanalytic training. Until recently, psychoanalytic educators tended to rely on a narrow and limited version of psychoanalysis characterized by a close adherence to Freud's papers on technique. However, clinical experience demanded modifications to Freud's technical recommendations so that clinician-teachers were faced with significant discrepancies between the realities of their practice and the ideals that guided their teaching. Supervision continued to be governed by this conservative trend, and the resulting discrepancies remained hidden and never adequately resolved. This tension between the conservative demands of analytic education and the modifications to technique and theory required by clinical experience was manifest by the absence, in the early literature on supervision, of material illustrating the actual events of supervision. In addition, the status quo was effectively maintained through the failure to examine, in detail, the basic assumptions of the prevailing models of supervision.

The breakthrough came with Ekstein and Wallerstein's book, The Teaching and Learning of Psychotherapy, first published in 1959. These authors expanded the theory of supervision beyond the mere didactic teaching of technique. They emphasized the significance of resolving the supervisee's learning problems in the context of the examination of his transference and countertransference issues. Equally significantly, they opened up psychoanalytic supervision for detailed examination by studying the actual interactions between supervisor and supervisee.

The Editors wish to acknowledge the editorial assistance of Rosalind Kindler in the preparation of the Prologue and Epilogue.

Analytic stalemate is a common experience in analytic practice. Some of the salient characteristics of analytic stalemates are well described in the dynamic relationship between Freud and the Wolf Man when the Wolf Man became preoccupied with his symptoms and stopped producing what Freud (1918) considered to be meaningful associations. In response, Freud set a time limit for the termination of the analysis; the Wolf Man soon realized that he was in earnest, and once more began to produce clinical material that allowed Freud to resume the analysis. Twenty years later, however, Freud (1937) returned to the Wolf Man as he reviewed portions of his analytic experiences, and was skeptical of using a termination date as a standard technique for overcoming analytic stalemate. He resorted to an ultimatum when he felt hopeless and emotionally exhausted, convinced that the patient had paralyzed the analytic process and that no interpretive effort on his part would have remobilized it.

Freud did not have the benefit of presenting his analytic stalemate to a consultant or supervisor.

Jean baker miller (1991) addresses the importance of ambition in women. She writes, in effect, that if we are going to create the kinds of institutions and personal lives that permit women to grow and flourish, we must apply much more conscious, concerted, direct attention to women and power. Miller adds that she believes most women still have a great deal of trouble with the issue and that we must continue to study this issue together. The topic is not only important, but also timely. For example, it is interesting to consider how the recent nomination and confirmation of a woman, Ruth Bader Ginsburg, as Associate Justice of the Supreme Court was responded to in the press. There was an enormous show of interest in her growth and development, with the focus on how she represents her entire generation of women in the degree to which her ascension to power seemed against all odds. To illustrate, Ginsburg (1993) told this story about herself.

At a tea given for her and the eight other women in her class at Harvard Law School in 1956, the Dean asked each woman in turn how she felt about taking a place earmarked for a man.

Emerging evidence indicates that males and females may follow distinct trajectories of emotional development. The male trajectory may be characterized by an emphasis on separateness and independence, whereas the female trajectory may be characterized by skillfulness in interpersonal relatedness. These differences begin during the first year of life, within the context of mother-child emotional communication. The consequence of these differences in early emotional experiences may be that males and females develop different modes of autonomous strivings—males becoming effective in independent, self-initiated activities and females becoming effective in relationship regulation.

We begin with a discussion of the concept of autonomy. We then present a review of the literature of sex differences in social relations, focusing on infancy and toddlerhood (encompassing the first three years of life) and childhood. A brief presentation of our own research, highlighting the role of emotional availability in organizing these sex differences during the transition from infancy to early childhood, will follow.
